relationship: Divine creation of all things
rationale: Sirach attributes the creation of all things to the one who lives for ever; Wisdom's prayer likewise addresses God as the maker of all things, expressly adding creation by His word.
source_text: He who lives for ever created all things together.

target_units.text: “God of the fathers and Lord of mercy, who made all things by Thy word

relationship: Divine vindication
rationale: Sirach declares that the Lord alone will be justified; Romans contrasts God's truth with human falsehood and quotes the declaration that God is justified in His words.
source_text: The Lord alone will be justified.

target_units.text: May it never be! But let God be true, and every human being a liar, just as it is written, “So that Thou mayest be justified in Thy words, and wilt prevail when Thou art judged.”

relationship: Unsearchable divine works
rationale: Sirach denies human ability to declare or trace God's mighty works fully; Job calls His great works unsearchable and beyond numbering.
source_text: He has empowered no one to declare His works fully; who will trace out His mighty deeds?

target_units.text: He does great and unsearchable things, glorious and extraordinary things beyond numbering.

relationship: Divine greatness and mercy beyond measure
rationale: Sirach asks who can count God's greatness and recount His mercies; the psalm describes His greatness as without limit and His mercy as abundant while recounting His mighty acts.
source_text: Who will count the might of His greatness? Who will go on to recount His mercies?

target_units.text: Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised; His greatness has no limit.
Generation after generation will praise Thy works, and they will declare Thy power.
They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of Thy holiness, and they will recount Thy wonders.
They will speak of the power of Thy fearsome acts, and they will recount Thy greatness.
They will pour forth remembrance of the abundance of Thy kindness and rejoice in Thy righteousness.
Compassionate and merciful is the Lord, patient and abundant in mercy.

relationship: Nothing added to or removed from God's work
rationale: Both passages deny the possibility of adding to or diminishing what God has done. Ecclesiastes additionally states that His work endures for ever.
source_text: It is impossible to diminish or to add, and impossible to trace out the Lord’s wonders.

target_units.text: I knew that everything God has done will endure for ever. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing taken from it; God has done this so that people may fear before Him.

relationship: Question about the human being's significance
rationale: Sirach asks what a human being is and what use or good belongs to him; the psalm asks what a human being is that God remembers and visits him.
source_text: What is a human being, and what is his use? What is his good, and what is his evil?

target_units.text: what is a human being, that Thou rememberest him, or a son of man, that Thou visitest him?

relationship: Contrasting estimates of a bounded human lifespan
rationale: Sirach describes a hundred years as many human years; the psalm speaks of seventy or, with strength, eighty. The numbers differ, but both reckon mortal life in a limited span of years.
source_text: The number of a person’s days, in many years, is a hundred.

target_units.text: The days of our years—in them are seventy years, or, with strength, eighty years; the greater part of them is toil and pain, for gentleness came upon us, and we shall be disciplined.

relationship: Human years set beside eternity
rationale: Sirach reduces human years to a drop or grain beside a day of eternity; the psalm compares a thousand years in God's eyes to a past day or night watch.
source_text: Like a drop of water from the sea or a grain of sand, so are a few years in a day of eternity.

target_units.text: For a thousand years in Thine eyes are like yesterday, which passed, and a watch in the night.

relationship: Mercy in view of human frailty
rationale: Sirach's description of short human life leads to the Lord's patience and mercy; the psalm joins His compassion to knowledge that people are dust and pass like grass.
source_text: Therefore the Lord was patient with them and poured His mercy upon them.

target_units.text: As a father has compassion on children, the Lord had compassion on those who fear Him,
for He knew our formation. Remember that we are dust.
A man—his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he will flower,
for a wind passed through him, and he will not exist, and he will no longer recognize his place.
But the Lord’s mercy is from eternity to eternity toward those who fear Him, and His righteousness toward children’s children,

relationship: Atonement and remembrance of mortality
rationale: Sirach connects God's knowledge of the grievous human end with increased atonement; the psalm joins His compassionate atonement to remembrance that people are passing flesh.
source_text: He saw and knew that their end was grievous; therefore He multiplied His atonement.

target_units.text: But He is compassionate; He will make atonement for their sins and not destroy, and will turn back His wrath again and again, and will not kindle all His anger.
And He remembered that they are flesh, a spirit going away and not returning.

relationship: Mercy extending beyond one's neighbor
rationale: Sirach contrasts limited human mercy with the Lord's mercy upon all flesh; the psalm likewise declares Him kind to all, with compassion over all His works. The target concerns this broad scope.
source_text: A person’s mercy is toward his neighbor, but the Lord’s mercy is upon all flesh: rebuking, disciplining, teaching, and bringing back like a shepherd his flock.

target_units.text: The Lord is kind to all, and His compassions are over all His works.

relationship: Divine favor and receptive discipline
rationale: Sirach associates mercy with receiving discipline; Proverbs urges the child not to reject the Lord's correction, because He disciplines the one He loves.
source_text: He has mercy on those who receive discipline and those who hasten eagerly toward His judgments.

target_units.text: Son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline or lose heart when corrected by Him,
for the Lord disciplines the one He loves and scourges every son He receives.

relationship: Giving without reproach
rationale: Sirach forbids adding reproach or hurtful words to a gift; James portrays God's generous giving as without reproach, supplying a positive example of that manner of giving.
source_text: Child, do not add reproach to good deeds, or the grief of words to any gift.

target_units.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

relationship: Beneficial words pictured through bodily relief
rationale: Sirach compares a good word's benefit to dew relieving heat; Proverbs compares good words to honeycombs whose sweetness heals life. Both give speech a restorative sensory image.
source_text: Will not dew bring relief from scorching heat? So a word is better than a gift.

target_units.text: Good words are honeycombs, and their sweetness is healing of the life.

relationship: Same-chapter union of gracious speech and giving
rationale: The earlier warning forbids hurtful words with gifts and praises a word's value; this verse draws the two together by locating both the good word and good gift in a gracious person.
source_text: Behold, is not a word beyond a good gift? Yet both are found with a gracious man.

target_units.text: Child, do not add reproach to good deeds, or the grief of words to any gift.
Will not dew bring relief from scorching heat? So a word is better than a gift.

relationship: The harm of begrudging generosity
rationale: Sirach depicts the distress caused by a grudging gift and graceless reproach; Proverbs warns against a begrudging host and describes the resulting ruin of good words.
source_text: A fool will reproach gracelessly, and a grudging person’s gift makes eyes waste away.

target_units.text: Do not dine with a begrudging man, and do not desire his foods,
for as if someone swallowed a hair, so he eats and drinks.
Do not bring him in to yourself and eat your morsel with him, for he will vomit it and ruin your good words.

relationship: Preparation before speaking
rationale: Sirach requires learning before speech; Proverbs condemns answering a matter before hearing it as foolishness and reproach. This supports the speech clause, not the separate medical advice.
source_text: Learn before speaking, and attend to your health before illness.

target_units.text: One who answers a word before hearing it—it is foolishness and reproach for him.

relationship: Self-examination before judgment
rationale: Sirach urges self-examination before visitation and judgment; Paul requires self-examination and says that discerning ourselves would avert judgment, within his specific teaching about the Lord's meal.
source_text: Examine yourself before judgment, and at the hour of visitation you will find atonement.

target_units.text: Let a person examine himself, and in this way let him eat from the bread and drink from the cup.
For the one who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment upon himself.
For this reason many among you are weak and ill, and a considerable number are asleep.
But if we discerned ourselves, we would not be judged.
Yet when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world.

relationship: Repentance and inward humbling
rationale: Sirach calls for humility and repentance while sin can be addressed; Joel calls for a whole-hearted return to God and the tearing of hearts. Neither link requires treating illness as a particular sin's result.
source_text: Humble yourself before you fall ill, and show repentance at the time of sins.

target_units.text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

relationship: Prompt fulfillment of a vow
rationale: Both warn against delaying payment of a vow. Ecclesiastes explicitly says it is better not to vow than to vow and fail to pay.
source_text: Do not be held back from repaying a vow at the right time, and do not wait until death to be justified.

target_units.text: Whenever you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for there is no delight in fools. Pay whatever you vow.
Better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay.

relationship: Deliberation before a vow
rationale: Sirach requires preparation before making a vow; Proverbs calls quick consecration a trap when reconsideration comes only after the vow.
source_text: Prepare yourself before making a vow, and do not become like a person testing the Lord.

target_units.text: It is a trap for a man quickly to consecrate something of his own, for after making the vow comes reconsideration.

relationship: Remembering wrath and retribution
rationale: Sirach directs attention to the coming time of wrath and retribution; Romans warns of stored-up wrath on the day of righteous judgment and repayment according to deeds.
source_text: Remember wrath in the days of death, and the time of retribution when the face is turned away.

target_units.text: But by your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment,
who will repay each according to his works:

relationship: Preparing for famine during abundance
rationale: Sirach tells the prosperous to remember famine and need; Joseph's plan to reserve food during abundant years for coming famine gives a concrete example of such foresight.
source_text: Remember a time of famine in a time of fullness, poverty and need in days of wealth.

target_units.text: “And let Pharaoh act, and appoint governors over the land; and let them take a fifth of all the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.
“And let them gather all the food of these seven good years which are coming; and let the grain be gathered under Pharaoh’s hand, and let food be kept in the cities.
“And the food shall be kept for the land against the seven years of famine which shall be in the land of Egypt, and the land shall not be destroyed by the famine.”

relationship: Uncertainty of changing days
rationale: Sirach emphasizes how quickly circumstances change between morning and evening; Proverbs forbids boasting about tomorrow because the coming day's outcome is unknown.
source_text: From morning until evening the time changes, and all things are swift before the Lord.

target_units.text: Do not boast of things for tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bear.

relationship: Wise caution turning from evil
rationale: Sirach's wise person guards against wrongdoing; Proverbs contrasts the wise person who fears and turns from evil with the self-confident fool who mixes with a lawless person.
source_text: A wise person will be cautious in everything, and in days of sins will guard against wrongdoing.

target_units.text: The wise, becoming afraid, turned from evil, but the fool, trusting himself, mixes with a lawless person.

relationship: Wisdom expressed in carefully formed sayings
rationale: Sirach associates understanding speech with producing precise proverbs; Ecclesiastes connects wisdom and teaching with an orderly arrangement of proverbs and the search for truthful, upright words.
source_text: Those understanding in words have themselves become wise and rained down precise proverbs.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.

relationship: Resisting the rule of desire
rationale: Sirach forbids following one's desires and commands restraint of appetites; Galatians similarly warns against fulfilling fleshly desire and contrasts it with walking by the Spirit.
source_text: Do not walk after your desires, and restrain your appetites.

target_units.text: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will certainly not fulfill the desire of the flesh.
For the flesh desires what is against the Spirit, and the Spirit what is against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you want.

relationship: The danger of yielding to desire
rationale: Sirach warns of the humiliating outcome of satisfying desire; Romans forbids letting sin reign through obedience to bodily desires. The shared issue is surrender to desire, not an identical stated penalty.
source_text: If you supply your soul with the satisfaction of desire, it will make you an object of your enemies’ gloating.

target_units.text: Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires;

relationship: Costly participation in feasting
rationale: Sirach warns that rejoicing in luxury can bind a person to contribute to it; Proverbs likewise warns against stretching oneself over contributions and purchases of meat.
source_text: Do not rejoice in great luxury, lest you be bound to contribute to it.

target_units.text: Do not be a wine-drinker, and do not stretch yourself over contributions and purchases of meat;

relationship: Feasting and impoverishment
rationale: Sirach warns against impoverishing oneself through borrowed feasts; Proverbs joins a warning about meal contributions to the poverty of the drunkard. Borrowing is Sirach's additional circumstance.
source_text: Do not become poor by feasting on borrowed money when you have nothing in your purse.

target_units.text: Do not be a wine-drinker, and do not stretch yourself over contributions and purchases of meat;
for every drunkard and frequenter of prostitutes will become poor, and every sleepy person will clothe himself in torn and ragged things.

relationship: Drunkenness and poverty
rationale: Sirach says a drunken worker will not become rich; Proverbs likewise predicts poverty for the drunkard. The link concerns the first clause, not the separate warning about despising small things.
source_text: A drunken worker will not become rich; the one who despises small things will fall little by little.

target_units.text: for every drunkard and frequenter of prostitutes will become poor, and every sleepy person will clothe himself in torn and ragged things.

relationship: Women, wine, and impaired judgment
rationale: Sirach warns that wine and women lead understanding men astray; the royal instruction warns against giving wealth to women and drinking so as to forget wisdom and fail in judgment.
source_text: Wine and women will lead understanding men astray, and the one who clings to prostitutes will become more reckless.

target_units.text: Do not give women your wealth, or your mind and livelihood to belated counsel.
Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel. The powerful are hot-tempered, but let them not drink wine,
so that, after drinking, they may not forget wisdom and become entirely unable to judge the weak rightly.

relationship: Worms as a mortal inheritance
rationale: Both use inheritance language for the association between death and worms. Chapter 10 applies it to human death generally, while this verse concludes a warning about reckless conduct.
source_text: Rot and worms will inherit him, and a reckless soul will be taken away.

target_units.text: For when a person dies, he will inherit creeping things, beasts, and worms.

relationship: Caution about ready belief
rationale: Sirach criticizes quick trust; Proverbs contrasts the person who believes every word with the resourceful person who reconsiders. This supports the warning about credulity.
source_text: The one who trusts quickly is lighthearted, and the one who sins will wrong his own soul.

target_units.text: The innocent person believes every word, but the resourceful comes to reconsideration.

relationship: Restrained speech limiting evil
rationale: Sirach says hatred of chatter diminishes evil; Proverbs says much talking does not escape sin and praises sparing one's lips.
source_text: but the one who hates chatter diminishes evil.

target_units.text: Through much talking you will not escape sin, but by sparing your lips you will be intelligent.

relationship: Keeping matters confidential
rationale: Sirach warns against repeating a word; Proverbs contrasts disclosure by a double-tongued person with a faithful person's concealment of matters.
source_text: Never repeat a word, and you will certainly lose nothing.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

relationship: Discretion about disclosure
rationale: Sirach forbids revealing a matter to friend or enemy unless silence would be sinful; Proverbs praises faithful concealment. Sirach expressly states an exception that the proverb does not discuss.
source_text: Do not tell it to friend or enemy, and unless silence is a sin for you, do not reveal it.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

relationship: Same-chapter consequence of indiscreet disclosure
rationale: The preceding commands forbid repeating and disclosing a word; this verse explains the danger through a hearer who keeps watch and later hates the speaker.
source_text: For someone has heard you and kept watch on you, and in time he will hate you.

target_units.text: Never repeat a word, and you will certainly lose nothing.
Do not tell it to friend or enemy, and unless silence is a sin for you, do not reveal it.

relationship: Allowing a heard matter to remain concealed
rationale: Sirach's instruction to let a heard word die with oneself corresponds to the faithful person's concealment of matters in Proverbs.
source_text: Have you heard a word? Let it die with you. Take courage; it will certainly not make you burst.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

relationship: Same-chapter painful images for an unrestrained word
rationale: The word troubling a fool is compared first to labor pains and then to an arrow fixed in flesh. Both images portray the fool's inability to bear a word quietly.
source_text: A fool will suffer labor pains over a word, like a woman giving birth over her baby.

target_units.text: An arrow fixed in the flesh of a thigh—so is a word in a fool’s belly.

relationship: Same-chapter bodily pain as a speech image
rationale: The arrow and belly image continues the preceding comparison of a fool's distress over a word to childbirth pains; the particular connection is the painful pressure of an uncontained word.
source_text: An arrow fixed in the flesh of a thigh—so is a word in a fool’s belly.

target_units.text: A fool will suffer labor pains over a word, like a woman giving birth over her baby.

relationship: Personal correction seeking a restored relationship
rationale: Sirach urges questioning a friend to establish what happened and prevent repetition; Matthew directs private reproof of a sinning brother with the aim of gaining him. Sirach additionally warns that the deed may not have occurred.
source_text: Question a friend; perhaps he did not do it, and if he did, question him so that he may not repeat it.

target_units.text: If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother.

relationship: Same-chapter questioning of alleged conduct and speech
rationale: The two instructions apply the same cautious questioning first to an alleged deed and then to alleged speech, allowing innocence and seeking to prevent repetition if the report is true.
source_text: Question your neighbor; perhaps he did not say it, and if he has said it, question him so that he may not say it again.

target_units.text: Question a friend; perhaps he did not do it, and if he did, question him so that he may not repeat it.

relationship: Testing reports instead of believing everything
rationale: Sirach warns that slander is frequent and forbids trusting every report; Proverbs contrasts believing every word with thoughtful reconsideration.
source_text: Question a friend, for slander often occurs; do not trust every report.

target_units.text: The innocent person believes every word, but the resourceful comes to reconsideration.

relationship: The common danger of stumbling in speech
rationale: Sirach asks who has not sinned with the tongue and allows unintended slips; James says all stumble in many things and makes freedom from stumbling in speech a mark of completeness.
source_text: There is someone who slips without intending it in his soul; who has not sinned with his tongue?

target_units.text: For we all stumble in many things. If anyone does not stumble in speech, that person is a complete man, able to bridle his whole body also.

relationship: Lawful correction instead of hostility
rationale: Sirach calls for questioning before threatening and giving place to God's law; Leviticus commands reproof of one's neighbor while forbidding hatred, vengeance, and lasting anger.
source_text: Question your neighbor before threatening him, and give place to the law of the Most High.

target_units.text: You shall not hate your brother in your mind; you shall surely reprove your neighbour, and you shall not bear sin because of him.
And your hand shall not take vengeance, neither shall you remain angry with the sons of your people; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the Lord.

relationship: Wisdom as reverence and obedient conduct
rationale: Sirach identifies wisdom with fear of the Lord and doing the law; Job identifies reverence for God with wisdom and abstention from evil with knowledge.
source_text: All wisdom is fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom there is doing the law.

target_units.text: And He said to a human, ‘Behold, reverence for God is wisdom, and abstaining from evils is knowledge.’”

relationship: Distinguishing wisdom from wicked cleverness
rationale: Sirach denies that knowledge of wickedness or sinful counsel is wisdom; James rejects jealous, self-seeking wisdom as earthly and demonic and contrasts it with pure, peaceable wisdom.
source_text: Knowledge of wickedness is not wisdom, and where sinners take counsel there is no prudence.

target_units.text: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, do not boast against the truth and lie against it.
This is not the wisdom coming down from above; it is earthly, merely natural, demonic.
For where there are jealousy and selfish ambition, there are disorder and every foul practice.
But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, considerate, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without hypocrisy.

relationship: A kind of cleverness unworthy of wisdom's name
rationale: Sirach allows for abhorrent shrewdness; James similarly distinguishes purported wisdom that is earthly and demonic from the pure wisdom from above.
source_text: There is shrewdness that is an abomination, and there is a foolish person deficient in wisdom.

target_units.text: This is not the wisdom coming down from above; it is earthly, merely natural, demonic.
For where there are jealousy and selfish ambition, there are disorder and every foul practice.
But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, considerate, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without hypocrisy.

relationship: Same-chapter priority of fear and obedience over cleverness
rationale: The preference for a less knowledgeable but God-fearing person over a lawbreaking expert follows the chapter's definition of wisdom as fear of the Lord and doing the law.
source_text: Better someone lacking understanding but full of fear than someone abounding in prudence who transgresses the law.

target_units.text: All wisdom is fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom there is doing the law.

relationship: Same-chapter rejection of unjust shrewdness
rationale: The first clause's precise but unjust shrewdness illustrates the earlier refusal to call knowledge of wickedness wisdom. The link does not resolve the separate clause about twisting matters to bring judgment to light.
source_text: There is precise shrewdness that is unjust, and there is someone who twists matters in order to bring a judgment to light.

target_units.text: Knowledge of wickedness is not wisdom, and where sinners take counsel there is no prudence.

relationship: Humble-looking behavior concealing deceit
rationale: Sirach describes gloomy, bowed-down conduct with deceit within; Proverbs describes an enemy's tears and agreeable lips while his heart devises deceit.
source_text: There is someone who acts wickedly while bowed down in gloom, with his inward parts full of deceit.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

relationship: Deceptive outward conduct
rationale: The concealed face and pretended deafness belong to Sirach's deceptive character portrait; Proverbs similarly warns that an enemy's outward entreaties can conceal inward evil.
source_text: Hiding his face and pretending to be deaf, where he has not been recognized he will get ahead of you.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

relationship: Circumstances preventing a sinful act
rationale: Lack of strength prevents sin here, while need prevents it in chapter 20. Sirach 19 adds an evil intention for a future opportunity; that intention is not imputed to the other passage.
source_text: If lack of strength prevents him from sinning, he will do evil when he finds an opportunity.

target_units.text: There is someone prevented from sinning by need; in his rest he will not be pierced with remorse.

relationship: Wisdom visible in the face
rationale: Sirach associates recognizing understanding with the look of a person's face; Ecclesiastes says wisdom lights up the face and contrasts a shameless face.
source_text: A man will be recognized from his appearance, and an understanding person from the look of his face.

target_units.text: Who knows wise people, and who knows the solution of a saying? A person’s wisdom will light up his face, but one with a shameless face will be hated.

relationship: Same-chapter expansion of visible character signs
rationale: After appearance and facial expression, the description adds clothing, the grin of the teeth, and one's steps as outward signs by which a person's character is recognized.
source_text: A man’s clothing, the grin of his teeth, and a person’s steps will declare what he is like.

target_units.text: A man will be recognized from his appearance, and an understanding person from the look of his face.

relationship: Prudent restraint in speech
rationale: Sirach contrasts an unfitting rebuke with prudent silence; Proverbs praises restraint of a harsh word and says someone who makes himself mute will seem intelligent.
source_text: There is a rebuke that is not fitting, and there is a silent person who is prudent.

target_units.text: One who refrains from sending forth a harsh word is discerning, and a patient man is intelligent.
Wisdom will be reckoned to a senseless person who asks for wisdom, and someone who makes himself mute will seem intelligent.

relationship: Reproof preferred to sustained anger
rationale: Sirach prefers rebuke to anger; Leviticus requires reproof of the neighbor while forbidding hatred and remaining angry with one's people.
source_text: How much better to rebuke than to be angry,

target_units.text: You shall not hate your brother in your mind; you shall surely reprove your neighbour, and you shall not bear sin because of him.
And your hand shall not take vengeance, neither shall you remain angry with the sons of your people; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the Lord.

relationship: Acknowledgment of wrongdoing
rationale: Sirach associates acknowledging fault with preservation from loss; 1 John calls for confession of sins and promises forgiveness and cleansing. The outcomes are stated differently.
source_text: and the one who acknowledges his fault will be kept from loss.

target_units.text: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

relationship: Silence and the appearance of wisdom
rationale: Both sayings associate silence with being regarded as wise or intelligent. Sirach adds the contrast of hatred caused by much chatter.
source_text: There is a silent person who is found wise, and there is someone hated for much chatter.

target_units.text: Wisdom will be reckoned to a senseless person who asks for wisdom, and someone who makes himself mute will seem intelligent.

relationship: Recognizing a time for silence
rationale: Sirach distinguishes inability to answer from knowing the right time to remain silent; Ecclesiastes explicitly gives both silence and speech their proper time.
source_text: There is someone silent because he has no answer, and someone silent because he knows the right time.

target_units.text: a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to be silent and a time to speak,

relationship: Speaking and keeping silent at the proper time
rationale: The wise person's waiting to speak corresponds to Ecclesiastes' recognition of a time to be silent and a time to speak; Sirach contrasts the fool who misses that time.
source_text: A wise person will keep silent until the right time, but a babbler and a fool will miss the right time.

target_units.text: a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to be silent and a time to speak,

relationship: The harmful multiplication of words
rationale: Sirach warns that multiplying words brings loathing; Ecclesiastes portrays the fool multiplying words while his own lips drown him. The connection concerns excess speech, not Sirach's separate authority clause.
source_text: The one who multiplies words will be loathed, and the one who assumes authority will be hated.

target_units.text: The words of a wise person’s mouth are gracious, but a fool’s lips will drown him.
The beginning of his mouth’s words is folly, and the end of his speech is evil wandering.
The fool multiplies words. A person did not know what happened, and who will tell him what will be after him?

relationship: Gain that turns into harm
rationale: Sirach allows for a gain that brings loss; Ecclesiastes describes wealth kept to its owner's harm and then lost through a grievous distraction.
source_text: There is success for a man amid adversity, and there is a gain that brings loss.

target_units.text: There is a sickness I have seen beneath the sun: wealth kept by its possessor to his harm,
and that wealth will be lost through a grievous distraction, and he fathered a son with nothing in his hand.

relationship: Elevation from lowliness
rationale: Sirach's second clause describes someone lifting his head from lowliness; James promises exaltation to those who humble themselves before the Lord. James supplies the explicitly religious setting.
source_text: There is loss for the sake of glory, and there is someone who has lifted his head from lowliness.

target_units.text: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.

relationship: Wise words winning favor
rationale: Sirach says the wise person makes himself welcome through words; Ecclesiastes describes a wise person's words as gracious and contrasts the self-destructive lips of a fool.
source_text: A wise person will make himself welcome by his words, but fools’ favors will be wasted.

target_units.text: The words of a wise person’s mouth are gracious, but a fool’s lips will drown him.

relationship: A gift or meal spoiled by the giver's disposition
rationale: Sirach rejects a gift whose giver seeks excessive return; Proverbs warns against dining with a begrudging person. Both expose apparent generosity that does not benefit the recipient.
source_text: An unthinking person’s gift will not benefit you, for his eyes seek many things in exchange for one.

target_units.text: Do not dine with a begrudging man, and do not desire his foods,
for as if someone swallowed a hair, so he eats and drinks.
Do not bring him in to yourself and eat your morsel with him, for he will vomit it and ruin your good words.

relationship: Same-chapter portrait of an ungenerous giver
rationale: The giver seeking many things for one gift is further portrayed as giving little, reproaching loudly, and demanding repayment almost immediately.
source_text: He will give little and reproach much, and open his mouth like a herald. Today he will lend, and tomorrow he will demand repayment; such a person is hateful.

target_units.text: An unthinking person’s gift will not benefit you, for his eyes seek many things in exchange for one.

relationship: Same-chapter contrast between complaint and conduct
rationale: The fool complains of having no friend or gratitude after the passage has described gifts demanding excessive return and reproach. The connection places his complaint beside the specific conduct that precedes it.
source_text: A fool will say, “I have no friend, and there is no gratitude for my good deeds.”

target_units.text: An unthinking person’s gift will not benefit you, for his eyes seek many things in exchange for one.
He will give little and reproach much, and open his mouth like a herald. Today he will lend, and tomorrow he will demand repayment; such a person is hateful.

relationship: Stumbling with the tongue
rationale: Sirach considers a slip of the tongue worse than a slip on the ground; James similarly uses stumbling in speech as an image of human moral failure.
source_text: Better a slip on the ground than a slip of the tongue; so the fall of the wicked will come swiftly.

target_units.text: For we all stumble in many things. If anyone does not stumble in speech, that person is a complete man, able to bridle his whole body also.

relationship: Same-chapter speech spoiled by poor timing
rationale: The untimely tale associated with a graceless person is followed by the rejected proverb a fool does not speak at its proper time. Both concern inappropriate verbal performance.
source_text: A graceless person is an untimely tale; it will be continually in the mouth of the uninstructed.

target_units.text: A proverb will be rejected from a fool’s mouth, for he will certainly not say it at its proper time.

relationship: A proverb unfitted to a fool's mouth
rationale: Sirach explains rejection of a fool's proverb through his failure to speak at the proper time; Proverbs also separates a proverb from the mouth of fools without supplying that particular explanation.
source_text: A proverb will be rejected from a fool’s mouth, for he will certainly not say it at its proper time.

target_units.text: Remove walking from legs, and a proverb from the mouth of fools.

relationship: External circumstances restraining sin
rationale: Need prevents sin in this verse, as lack of strength does in chapter 19. Only the earlier passage explicitly adds an intention to do evil when opportunity comes.
source_text: There is someone prevented from sinning by need; in his rest he will not be pierced with remorse.

target_units.text: If lack of strength prevents him from sinning, he will do evil when he finds an opportunity.

relationship: Fearful regard for people causing a fall
rationale: Sirach warns that shame and regard for a foolish person can destroy one's soul; Proverbs describes people tripped up by fear and shame before others, in the setting of failing to report wrongdoing.
source_text: There is someone who destroys his soul through shame, and through regard for a foolish face he will lose it.

target_units.text: One who shares with a thief hates his own life; but if, when an oath is set before them, those who heard do not report,
having feared and felt shame before people, they were tripped up; but one who trusts in the Lord will rejoice. Impiety gives a man a fall; but one who trusts in the Master will be saved.

relationship: Condemnation of lying speech
rationale: Sirach calls a lie an evil blemish that repeatedly appears in uninstructed speech; Proverbs calls lying lips an abomination to the Lord.
source_text: A lie is an evil blemish in a person; it will be continually in the mouth of the uninstructed.

target_units.text: Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but one who performs faithful deeds is acceptable to Him.

relationship: Destruction overtaking theft and false speech
rationale: Sirach says both theft and persistent lying end in destruction; Zechariah's curse brings death and destruction upon thieves and false swearers. False swearing is the target's particular form of falsehood.
source_text: A thief is preferable to someone who persists in lying, but both will inherit destruction.

target_units.text: He said to me, “This is the curse going out over the whole earth, because every thief will be punished by this with death, and every false swearer will be punished by this with death.

I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty. It will enter the thief’s house and the house of whoever swears falsely by My name; it will lodge within his house and destroy it completely, its timbers and its stones.”

relationship: Falsehood and shame
rationale: Sirach associates a liar's character with dishonor and continuing shame; Proverbs contrasts the righteous person's hatred of an unjust word with the impious person's shame and loss of frankness.
source_text: A lying person’s character is dishonor, and his shame is continually with him.

target_units.text: The righteous hates an unjust word, but the impious is ashamed and will have no frankness.

relationship: Speech finding favor with rulers
rationale: Sirach connects wise speech with advancement and pleasing dignitaries; Proverbs says righteous lips are acceptable to a king and that he loves upright words.
source_text: A wise person will advance himself through his words, and a prudent man will please dignitaries.

target_units.text: Righteous lips are acceptable to a king, and he loves upright words.

relationship: Working the land and receiving food
rationale: Sirach's cultivator raises a heap of grain; Proverbs says the worker of his own land will be filled with loaves. The link concerns cultivation, not the separate clause about pleasing dignitaries.
source_text: The one who works the land will raise his heap of grain, and the one who pleases dignitaries will atone for injustice.

target_units.text: One who works his own land will be filled with loaves, but those who pursue empty things lack understanding.

relationship: Gifts blinding judgment
rationale: Both explicitly say gifts blind the eyes and interfere with right speech or correction. Exodus prohibits receiving such gifts; Sirach illustrates their silencing effect with a muzzle.
source_text: Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise and turn aside rebukes like a muzzle in the mouth.

target_units.text: And you shall receive no gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of those who see, and corrupt righteous words.

relationship: Repeated hidden-wisdom and unseen-treasure saying
rationale: The later passage repeats the question about the benefit of hidden wisdom and unseen treasure, preserving the paired images and the challenge about their usefulness.
source_text: Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what benefit is there in either?

target_units.text: Children, preserve instruction in peace. But hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what benefit is there in either?

relationship: Repeated preference for hiding folly rather than wisdom
rationale: Both passages state the same comparison: the person concealing foolishness is better than the person concealing wisdom.
source_text: Better a person who hides his foolishness than a person who hides his wisdom.

target_units.text: A person who hides his foolishness is better than a person who hides his wisdom.

relationship: Repentance and prayer over committed sin
rationale: Sirach calls for ceasing to add sins and praying concerning earlier ones; Peter likewise tells Simon to repent of his wickedness and plead with the Lord for forgiveness.
source_text: Child, have you sinned? Do not add to it any more, and pray concerning your earlier sins.

target_units.text: Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and plead with the Lord that perhaps the intention of your heart may be forgiven you.

relationship: Fleeing sin rather than approaching it
rationale: Sirach commands flight from sin because it attacks and destroys; Paul commands flight from sexual immorality and identifies its harm to one's own body. Sexual immorality is the target's specific case.
source_text: Flee from sin as from the presence of a snake, for if you approach it, it will bite you. Its teeth are lions’ teeth, destroying human lives.

target_units.text: Flee sexual immorality. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.

relationship: Sin's deadly two-edged blade image
rationale: Sirach compares lawlessness to an incurably wounding two-edged sword; Proverbs uses a two-edged blade for the bitter outcome of involvement with a prostitute and describes the path to death and Hades.
source_text: All lawlessness is like a two-edged sword; there is no healing for its wound.

target_units.text: Afterward, however, you will find it more bitter than gall and sharper than a two-edged blade.
For folly’s feet lead those who engage with her down with death into Hades; her tracks are not firmly set.

relationship: The destruction of the proud person's house
rationale: Sirach predicts the wasting of the proud person's house; Proverbs explicitly says the Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent.
source_text: Intimidation and insolence will lay wealth waste; so the house of a proud person will be laid waste.

target_units.text: The Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent, but He established the boundary of a widow.

relationship: The poor person's cry heard by the Lord
rationale: Sirach describes the poor petitioner's words reaching God's ears; the psalm recounts a poor man's cry being heard and his rescue from afflictions.
source_text: A poor person’s petition goes from his mouth to His ears, and His judgment comes swiftly.

target_units.text: This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him; from all his afflictions He saved him.

relationship: Hatred of correction
rationale: Sirach puts hatred of rebuke on the sinner's path and contrasts a receptive fear of God; Proverbs contrasts love of discipline with the foolishness of hating rebukes.
source_text: The one who hates rebuke is in a sinner’s tracks, but the one who fears the Lord will turn back in heart.

target_units.text: One who loves discipline loves discernment, but one who hates rebukes is foolish.

relationship: A house endangered by another's resources
rationale: Sirach likens building with others' money to collecting stones for a storm; Habakkuk condemns accumulating what is not one's own and acquiring evil gain for a house that will suffer shame.
source_text: The one who builds his house with others’ money is like someone gathering its stones for a storm.

target_units.text: Will not all these take up a parable against him and a riddle for his account? They will say, ‘Woe to the one multiplying for himself what is not his—how long?—and heavily weighting his collar!’
For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.
Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.
O you who acquire evil gain for your house, setting your nest on high to escape the hand of evils!
You planned shame for your house, brought many peoples to an end, and your soul sinned.
For a stone will cry from a wall, and a beetle from wood will utter these things.

relationship: The lawless as tow consumed by fire
rationale: Both describe lawless people through the image of tow ending in fire. Isaiah adds sparks from their works and the absence of anyone to quench the burning.
source_text: An assembly of the lawless is gathered tow, and their end is a flame of fire.

target_units.text: Their strength will become a stalk of tow and their works sparks of fire. The lawless and sinners will be burned together, with no one to quench.”

relationship: An attractive road ending in Hades
rationale: Sirach's smoothly paved sinners' road ends in the pit of Hades; Proverbs warns of a way that seems upright but ends at the bottom of Hades.
source_text: The sinners’ road is smoothed with stones, but at its end is the pit of Hades.

target_units.text: There is a way that seems upright to people, but its final outcome comes to the bottom of Hades.

relationship: Wisdom, fear of God, and the law
rationale: Sirach 19 identifies wisdom with fear of the Lord and doing the law; this verse again joins keeping the law with wisdom as the fulfillment of that fear.
source_text: The one who keeps the law masters his thoughts, and wisdom is the fulfillment of the fear of the Lord.

target_units.text: All wisdom is fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom there is doing the law.

relationship: Shrewdness with a harmful character
rationale: The warning that some shrewdness multiplies bitterness corresponds to the earlier statement that there is shrewdness which is an abomination. Both refuse to treat cleverness alone as sufficient wisdom.
source_text: The one who is not shrewd will not be instructed, yet there is a shrewdness that multiplies bitterness.

target_units.text: There is shrewdness that is an abomination, and there is a foolish person deficient in wisdom.

relationship: Wise instruction as a spring of life
rationale: Sirach compares the wise person's counsel to a spring of life; Proverbs calls the wise person's law a fountain of life. The life-giving water image is shared.
source_text: A wise person’s knowledge will increase like a flood, and his counsel is like a spring of life.

target_units.text: The law of a wise person is a fountain of life, but the senseless will die by a trap.

relationship: Broken pottery and the failure to instruct a fool
rationale: Sirach depicts the fool's inability to retain knowledge as a broken vessel; the next chapter compares teaching a fool to gluing a potsherd together.
source_text: A fool’s inward parts are like a broken vessel; he will retain no knowledge.

target_units.text: The one teaching a fool is gluing a potsherd together, waking a sleeper from deep sleep.

relationship: The wise learner receives and increases instruction
rationale: Sirach's knowledgeable hearer praises and adds to a wise word; Proverbs says the wise person responds to reproof with love and becomes wiser when given a starting point. Both contrast receptive wisdom with resistance.
source_text: If a knowledgeable person hears a wise word, he will praise it and add to it. A self-indulgent person heard it, and it displeased him; he cast it behind his back.

target_units.text: Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.
Give a wise person a starting point, and he will be wiser; inform a righteous person, and he will receive still more.

relationship: Grace in an understanding person's speech
rationale: Sirach contrasts the burden of a fool's explanation with grace on an understanding lip; Ecclesiastes likewise calls wise words gracious and contrasts the fool's harmful lips.
source_text: A fool’s explanation is like a burden on a journey, but grace will be found on an understanding person’s lip.

target_units.text: The words of a wise person’s mouth are gracious, but a fool’s lips will drown him.

relationship: Attentive reception of wise counsel
rationale: Sirach describes an assembly seeking and considering the prudent person's words; Job remembers hearers attending silently to his counsel and awaiting his speech like thirsty earth awaiting rain.
source_text: The mouth of a prudent person will be sought in the assembly, and they will consider his words in their heart.

target_units.text: When they heard me, they paid attention and kept silent at my counsel.
They added nothing to my word, and became overjoyed whenever I spoke to them.
Like thirsty earth awaiting rain, so they awaited my speech.

relationship: Contrasting responses to instruction's bonds
rationale: The senseless experience instruction as fetters and handcuffs; chapter 6 tells the learner to accept wisdom's fetters and promises that her bonds will become shelter, glory, and gladness.
source_text: Instruction is fetters on the feet of the senseless, and like handcuffs on his right hand.

target_units.text: Put your feet into her fetters and your neck into her collar.
Place your shoulder beneath her and carry her, and do not resent her bonds.
Approach her with all your soul, and keep her ways with your whole strength.
Trace her out and seek her, and she will become known to you; when you have gained hold of her, do not let her go.
For in the end you will find her rest, and she will turn to gladness for you.
Her fetters will become a strong shelter for you, and her collars a robe of glory.
For there is a golden ornament upon her, and her bonds are a blue thread.

relationship: The sound of foolish laughter
rationale: Sirach contrasts a fool's loud laughter with a prudent person's quiet smile; Ecclesiastes likens foolish laughter to crackling thorns beneath a cauldron and calls it futility.
source_text: A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a shrewd man will barely smile quietly.

target_units.text: for like the sound of thorns beneath a cauldron, so is the laughter of fools. This too is futility.

relationship: Instruction worn as a precious ornament
rationale: Instruction is a golden ornament and bracelet for the prudent here; chapter 6 likewise describes wisdom with a golden ornament, glorious clothing, and a crown of rejoicing.
source_text: Instruction is like a golden ornament to the prudent, and like a bracelet on his right arm.

target_units.text: Her fetters will become a strong shelter for you, and her collars a robe of glory.
For there is a golden ornament upon her, and her bonds are a blue thread.
You will put her on as a robe of glory and place a crown of rejoicing upon yourself.

relationship: Restraint when entering another's space
rationale: Sirach contrasts the fool's hurried entrance into a house with an experienced person's reserve; Proverbs advises bringing one's foot rarely to a friend lest the friend become filled with one's presence and respond with hatred.
source_text: A fool’s foot is quick to enter a house, but an experienced person will feel shame before it.

target_units.text: Bring your foot rarely to your own friend, lest he become filled with you and hate you.

relationship: Same-chapter restraint at another person's house
rationale: The contrast between hasty entry and experienced reserve is sharpened into the contrast between peering through the door and respectfully standing outside.
source_text: A foolish person peers into a house from its door, but an instructed man will stand outside.

target_units.text: A fool’s foot is quick to enter a house, but an experienced person will feel shame before it.

relationship: Same-chapter respect for a household's boundary
rationale: Peering into a house and listening at its door are successive examples of uninstructed intrusion; the instructed person stands outside and recognizes the dishonor of such conduct.
source_text: It is a person’s lack of instruction to listen at a door, but the prudent will feel weighed down by the dishonor.

target_units.text: A foolish person peers into a house from its door, but an instructed man will stand outside.

relationship: Deliberate assessment of one's words
rationale: Sirach depicts prudent words as weighed in a balance; Proverbs describes the wise heart understanding what comes from its own mouth and carrying discernment on its lips.
source_text: Strangers’ lips will talk about these things, but the words of the prudent will be weighed in a balance.

target_units.text: A wise person’s heart will understand what comes from his own mouth, and will carry discernment upon his lips.

relationship: The whisperer's destructive speech
rationale: Sirach condemns the whisperer's self-staining conduct and local hatred; chapter 28 names whispering and double speech as destroyers of peaceful people and causes of unrest.
source_text: The whisperer stains his own soul and will be hated where he dwells.

target_units.text: Curse a whisperer and someone double-tongued, for he has destroyed many who were at peace.
A third tongue has shaken many and scattered them from nation to nation; it has pulled down fortified cities and overthrown dignitaries’ houses.
A third tongue has driven out courageous women and deprived them of their labors.
The one who attends to it will certainly not find rest or dwell in quiet.

relationship: Same-chapter repulsive images of laziness
rationale: The comparison of the lazy person to a filthy stone is followed by a comparison to dung. The two images portray others' disgust without requiring a claim that the objects are identical.
source_text: A lazy person has been compared to a filthy stone, and everyone will hiss at his dishonor.

target_units.text: A lazy person has been compared to a lump of dung; everyone who picks it up will shake his hand.

relationship: Same-chapter disgust at laziness
rationale: The dung image and the hand shaken after contact continue the preceding filthy-stone image and the public dishonor of the lazy person.
source_text: A lazy person has been compared to a lump of dung; everyone who picks it up will shake his hand.

target_units.text: A lazy person has been compared to a filthy stone, and everyone will hiss at his dishonor.

relationship: Parental sorrow over an uninstructed child
rationale: Sirach calls begetting an uninstructed child a father's shame; Proverbs says a father does not rejoice over an uneducated son. The connection concerns that clause, not the separate statement about a daughter.
source_text: A father’s shame is in begetting an uninstructed child, and a daughter brings about loss.

target_units.text: and a fool’s heart is pain to the one who possesses it. A father does not rejoice over an uneducated son, but an intelligent son gladdens his mother.

relationship: A child's conduct affecting the parent
rationale: Sirach contrasts the prudent daughter with one who brings parental grief; Proverbs similarly contrasts a wise son who gladdens his father with a foolish son who grieves his mother. The target does not explain inheriting a husband.
source_text: A prudent daughter will inherit her husband, but one who brings shame brings grief to her parent.

target_units.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is grief to his mother.

relationship: A wife's harmful conduct within marriage
rationale: Sirach describes a shameless woman's dishonor to father and husband; Proverbs contrasts a courageous wife with an evil-doing woman who destroys a man like a worm in wood.
source_text: A shameless woman shames both father and husband and will be dishonored by both.

target_units.text: A courageous woman is a crown to her husband; but as a worm in wood, so a woman who does evil destroys a man.

relationship: Recognizing the proper occasion for mourning and joy
rationale: Sirach compares untimely discourse to music during mourning; Ecclesiastes distinguishes times for weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing. This concerns appropriate occasions, not Sirach's separate commendation of discipline.
source_text: An untimely discourse is music in mourning, but lashes and discipline are wisdom at every time.

target_units.text: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to beat the breast in mourning and a time to dance,

relationship: The fool and broken pottery as a learning image
rationale: Teaching the fool is compared to repairing a potsherd, corresponding to the earlier description of the fool's inward parts as a broken vessel that cannot retain knowledge.
source_text: The one teaching a fool is gluing a potsherd together, waking a sleeper from deep sleep.

target_units.text: A fool’s inward parts are like a broken vessel; he will retain no knowledge.

relationship: Speech wasted on a foolish hearer
rationale: Sirach's drowsy fool fails to take in what has been said; Proverbs forbids speaking into a fool's ears because he will sneer at intelligent words. The failures differ, but both concern an unreceptive hearer.
source_text: The one speaking to a fool is speaking to someone drowsy; at the end he will say, “What is it?”

target_units.text: Say nothing into a fool’s ears, lest he sneer at your intelligent words.

relationship: The dead person's rest tempering grief
rationale: Sirach gives the dead person's rest as a reason for gentler weeping; chapter 38 similarly calls for comfort and the resting of remembrance when the dead person rests. This addresses the consolation clause, not the whole comparison with a fool.
source_text: Weep over a dead person, for he has lost the light; weep also over a fool, for he has lost understanding. Weep more gently over the dead, because he has found rest, but the fool’s life is worse than death.

target_units.text: When the dead person rests, bring his remembrance to rest, and be comforted concerning him when his spirit departs.

relationship: Seven days of mourning
rationale: Sirach names seven days as the period of mourning for the dead; Genesis records Joseph mourning his father for seven days. The narrative illustrates that duration, not the lifelong grief over a fool.
source_text: Mourning for the dead lasts seven days; for a fool and an ungodly person, all the days of his life.

target_units.text: And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan; and they lamented him with a great and exceedingly grievous lamentation, and he mourned his father seven days.

relationship: Avoiding fruitless speech with a fool
rationale: Sirach warns against multiplying words with someone without understanding; Proverbs likewise forbids speaking into a fool's ears because intelligent words will meet contempt.
source_text: Do not multiply words with a fool or go to someone without understanding. Guard against him so that you do not have trouble, and you will certainly not be stained by what he shakes off. Turn away from him, and you will find rest and will certainly not grow weary of his madness.

target_units.text: Say nothing into a fool’s ears, lest he sneer at your intelligent words.

relationship: The fool as an exceptionally heavy burden
rationale: Sirach calls the fool heavier than lead; Proverbs calls a fool's anger heavier than stone and sand. The materials and scope differ, but the disproportionate weight image is shared.
source_text: What is heavier than lead? What is its name except a fool?

target_units.text: A stone is heavy and sand hard to carry, but a fool’s anger is heavier than both.

relationship: The fool outweighing heavy materials
rationale: Sirach finds sand, salt, and iron easier to bear than an uncomprehending person; Proverbs similarly compares stone and sand with the still heavier anger of a fool.
source_text: Sand, salt, and a lump of iron are easier to bear than a person without understanding.

target_units.text: A stone is heavy and sand hard to carry, but a fool’s anger is heavier than both.

relationship: Wise understanding pictured as a stable building
rationale: Sirach compares a heart established on counsel to a fitted wooden bond that withstands shaking; Jesus compares hearing and doing His words to a prudent builder whose house withstands wind and water.
source_text: A wooden bond fitted into a building will not be loosened in a shaking; so a heart established on thoughtful counsel will not be cowardly when the time comes.

target_units.text: Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and puts them into practice will be likened to a prudent man who built his house upon the rock.
The rain came down, the rivers came, and the winds blew and fell upon that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon the rock.

relationship: Same-chapter architectural images of a firm heart
rationale: The heart established through understanding is depicted first through a fitted structural bond and then through an ornament on a polished wall. Both images concern a heart made firm by thought or counsel.
source_text: A heart made firm upon an understanding thought is like a sanded ornament on a polished wall.

target_units.text: A wooden bond fitted into a building will not be loosened in a shaking; so a heart established on thoughtful counsel will not be cowardly when the time comes.

relationship: Folly exposed by a destructive storm
rationale: Sirach likens a fearful heart resting on foolish thought to stakes unable to withstand wind; Jesus compares failure to act on His words to a foolish builder whose house falls when the storm strikes.
source_text: Stakes set on a height will certainly not endure before the wind; so a cowardly heart resting on a foolish thought will certainly not endure before any fear.

target_units.text: And everyone who hears these words of Mine and does not put them into practice will be likened to a foolish man who built his house upon the sand.
The rain came down, the rivers came, and the winds blew and struck that house, and it fell; and its fall was great.”

relationship: Reproach and the breaking of friendship
rationale: Sirach says reproaching a friend drives friendship away like stones scattering birds; Proverbs contrasts concealing wrongdoings to seek friendship with exposing them in a way that separates friends.
source_text: Throwing a stone at birds drives them away, and the one who reproaches a friend will break up friendship.

target_units.text: One who hides wrongdoings seeks friendship, but one who hates hiding them separates friends and household members.

relationship: The possibility of reconciliation after hostility
rationale: Sirach tells someone who has drawn a sword against a friend not to despair of a way back; Jesus directs a person whose brother has a grievance to seek reconciliation before presenting a gift.
source_text: If you draw a sword against a friend, do not despair, for there is a way back.

target_units.text: If therefore you offer your gift upon the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

relationship: Disclosure of secrets as a grave breach of friendship
rationale: Sirach distinguishes reparable hostile speech from breaches that drive a friend away, including disclosed secrets; chapter 27 likewise allows reconciliation after abuse but treats betrayed secrets as destroying trust and hope.
source_text: If you open your mouth against a friend, do not be afraid, for there is reconciliation—except for reproach, pride, disclosure of a secret, and a treacherous blow; at these things every friend will flee.

target_units.text: The one who reveals secrets has destroyed trust and will certainly not find a friend close to his soul.
Love a friend and keep faith with him; but if you reveal his secrets, do not pursue him afterward.
For as a person has lost his dead, so you have lost your neighbor’s friendship.
As you have released a bird from your hand, so you have let your neighbor go, and you will not catch him.
Do not pursue him, because he has gone far away and escaped like a gazelle from a trap.
For a wound can be bound up, and there is reconciliation after abuse, but the one who revealed secrets has lost hope.

relationship: Friendship maintained in adversity
rationale: Sirach urges faithfulness to a neighbor in poverty and affliction; Proverbs calls for a friend at all times and for brothers to be useful in need.
source_text: Establish trust with your neighbor in poverty, so that you may be filled together with him in his good circumstances. Stay with him in a time of affliction, so that you may share his inheritance.

target_units.text: Let a friend be yours at all times, and let brothers be useful in times of need; for this is why they are born.

relationship: Inflammatory words preceding conflict
rationale: Sirach says insults precede bloodshed as smoke precedes fire; Proverbs says a painful word stirs up anger and contrasts a yielding answer that turns wrath away.
source_text: Before fire come a furnace’s vapor and smoke; so before bloodshed come insults.

target_units.text: Anger destroys even intelligent people; but a yielding answer turns away wrath, and a painful word stirs up anger.

relationship: Refusing to abandon a friend
rationale: Sirach declares willingness to shelter a friend without hiding from him; Proverbs directly forbids abandoning one's friend or an ancestral friend.
source_text: I will not be ashamed to shelter a friend, and I will certainly not hide from his face.

target_units.text: Do not abandon your friend or an ancestral friend, and do not enter your brother’s house when misfortune strikes you; a nearby friend is better than a brother dwelling far away.

relationship: Prayer for a guard over the mouth
rationale: Both ask for a guard upon the mouth and protection around the lips. Sirach describes a skillful seal, while the psalm describes a restraining door.
source_text: Who will place a guard upon my mouth and a skillful seal upon my lips, so that I do not fall because of it and my tongue destroy me?

target_units.text: Set a guard, Lord, for my mouth and a restraining door around my lips.

relationship: Prayer against being led into sinful speech
rationale: Following the request to guard the mouth, Sirach asks God not to abandon him to their counsel or let him fall through them; the psalm also joins a guarded mouth to prayer against a heart turned toward wicked words.
source_text: Lord, Father and Master of my life, do not abandon me to their counsel; do not let me fall through them.

target_units.text: Set a guard, Lord, for my mouth and a restraining door around my lips.
Do not turn my heart toward words of wickedness, to offer excuses for sins with people who practice lawlessness, and I will certainly not join with their chosen ones.

relationship: Welcoming corrective discipline
rationale: Sirach seeks discipline over thought and heart so that errors are not spared; the psalm welcomes a righteous person's merciful discipline and correction.
source_text: Who will set lashes over my thought and wisdom’s discipline over my heart, so that they may not spare my errors of ignorance, and He may certainly not pass over their sins,

target_units.text: A righteous man will discipline me in mercy and correct me, but let a sinner’s oil not enrich my head, for still my prayer is amid their good pleasures.

relationship: Sin, stumbling, and enemies' gloating
rationale: Sirach prays that multiplying sins not cause a fall before gloating enemies; the psalm joins concern over lawlessness to the plea that enemies not rejoice when the speaker's feet are shaken.
source_text: so that my errors of ignorance do not multiply and my sins increase, and I fall before my adversaries and my enemy gloat over me?

target_units.text: For I said, “Let my enemies never rejoice over me!” When my feet were shaken, they boasted against me.
For I am ready for scourges, and my pain is continually before me.
For I will announce my lawlessness and be concerned about my sin.

relationship: Rejecting haughty eyes
rationale: Sirach asks God not to give him haughty eyes; the psalmist declares that his eyes were not raised high and his heart was not exalted.
source_text: Lord, Father and God of my life, do not give me haughty eyes,

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. For David. Lord, my heart was not exalted, nor were my eyes raised high; I did not walk among great things nor among wonders beyond me.

relationship: Prayer for desire to be redirected
rationale: Sirach asks that desire be turned away; the psalm asks God to bend the heart away from greed and turn the eyes from futility toward His way.
source_text: and turn desire away from me.

target_units.text: Bend my heart toward Thy testimonies, and not toward greed.
Turn away my eyes so that they do not see futility; give me life in Thy way.

relationship: Resisting bodily and sexual appetites
rationale: Sirach asks not to be overcome by belly and sexual appetite; Romans forbids revelry, drunkenness, and sexual promiscuity and rejects provision for fleshly desires.
source_text: Do not let the appetite of the belly and sexual intercourse overtake me, and do not hand me over to a shameless soul.

target_units.text: Let us walk honorably as in daytime, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and licentiousness, not in strife and jealousy;
but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh to satisfy its desires.

relationship: Guarded speech preserving life
rationale: Sirach promises that the keeper of mouth-discipline will not be caught; Proverbs says guarding one's mouth preserves life and contrasts rash lips.
source_text: Listen, children, to discipline of the mouth; the one who keeps it will certainly not be caught.

target_units.text: One who guards his own mouth keeps his own life, but one rash with his lips will terrify himself.

relationship: A sinner trapped through speech
rationale: Both explicitly describe a sinner falling into a trap through the lips. Sirach additionally names abusive and proud speakers as stumbling through them.
source_text: A sinner will be caught by his lips, and an abusive person and a proud person will stumble through them.

target_units.text: Through the sin of lips a sinner falls into traps, but the righteous escapes from them.

relationship: Restraint from habitual oaths
rationale: Sirach warns against accustoming the mouth to oaths; James commands plain yes and no instead of swearing and connects the warning with judgment.
source_text: Do not accustom your mouth to an oath, and do not make a habit of naming the Holy One.

target_units.text: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your yes be yes, and your no be no, so that you may not fall under judgment.

relationship: Invoking God's name and accountability for sin
rationale: Sirach warns that continual swearing and invoking the name will not leave a person cleansed from sin; Exodus refuses acquittal to someone who takes the Lord's name in vain. The target specifically addresses vain invocation.
source_text: For just as a household slave under continual examination will not be free of bruises, so the one who continually swears and invokes the name will certainly not be cleansed from sin.

target_units.text: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord shall by no means hold him guiltless who takes His name in vain.

relationship: False swearing bringing calamity upon a house
rationale: Sirach warns that vain or offending oaths fill a house with calamities; Zechariah describes the curse entering and destroying the false swearer's house.
source_text: A man of many oaths will be filled with lawlessness, and a scourge will not depart from his house. If he offends, his sin is upon him; if he disregards it, he has sinned twice. If he swore in vain, he will not be justified, for his house will be filled with calamities.

target_units.text: He said to me, “This is the curse going out over the whole earth, because every thief will be punished by this with death, and every false swearer will be punished by this with death.

I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty. It will enter the thief’s house and the house of whoever swears falsely by My name; it will lodge within his house and destroy it completely, its timbers and its stones.”

relationship: Rejecting crude and foolish speech
rationale: Sirach forbids making crude ignorance a habit of the mouth because sinful speech lies in it; Ephesians rejects shamefulness, foolish talk, and coarse joking as unfitting.
source_text: Do not accustom your mouth to crude ignorance, for sinful speech is in it.

target_units.text: nor shamefulness and foolish talk or coarse joking, which are unfitting, but rather thanksgiving.

relationship: Cursing the day of one's birth
rationale: Sirach describes birth-regret and a curse on one's birth day as a possible result of public foolishness; Job actually curses his birth day in suffering. The particular expression is shared, while its circumstances differ.
source_text: Remember your father and mother, for you sit among dignitaries, lest you forget yourself before them and become foolish through your habit; then you will wish you had not been born and curse the day of your birth.

target_units.text: After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day,
saying:
“May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which they said, ‘Behold, a male child!’

relationship: Same-chapter harmful habits of speech
rationale: The warning against habitual crude speech is extended to a person habituated to reproach who remains uninstructed. Both focus on speech becoming an entrenched habit.
source_text: A person accustomed to words of reproach will certainly not be instructed throughout all his days.

target_units.text: Do not accustom your mouth to crude ignorance, for sinful speech is in it.

relationship: Sexual misconduct pictured as consuming fire
rationale: Sirach places the heated soul's consuming fire beside the sexually immoral man's kindled fire; Proverbs compares involvement with a married woman to carrying fire or walking on burning coals without escaping injury.
source_text: a heated soul, like a burning fire, will certainly not be quenched until it is consumed; a sexually immoral man in his fleshly body will certainly not stop until he kindles a fire. Every loaf is sweet to a sexually immoral man; he will certainly not cease until he dies.

target_units.text: Will someone bind fire in his bosom without burning his garments?
Or will someone walk on fiery coals without burning his feet?
So is the one who goes in to a married woman: he will not be acquitted, nor will anyone touching her.

relationship: The adulterer relying on darkness for concealment
rationale: Both give the adulterer's claim that no one will see him in darkness. Job also describes concealing the face; Sirach exposes the further mistaken assumption that God will not remember.
source_text: A man who transgresses from his marriage bed says in his soul, “Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls cover me; no one sees me. What should I fear? The Most High will certainly not remember my sins.”

target_units.text: The adulterer’s eye watched for darkness, saying, ‘No eye will notice me,’ and he made a concealment for his face.

relationship: God's eyes observing every human way
rationale: Sirach denies that hidden places conceal misconduct from the Lord's eyes; Proverbs says a man's ways are before God's eyes and that He watches all his tracks, in a warning about another woman.
source_text: Human eyes are what he fears; he does not know that the Lord’s eyes are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, surveying every human way and observing hidden places.

target_units.text: For a man’s ways are before God’s eyes, and He watches all his tracks.

relationship: Divine knowledge before formation
rationale: Sirach states God's knowledge of all things before their creation; God's declaration that He knows Jeremiah before forming him supplies a particular instance of prior knowledge.
source_text: Before all things were created, they were known to Him, and likewise after they were completed.

target_units.text: Before I formed you in the belly, I know you; before you came out of the womb, I have consecrated you. I have appointed you a prophet to nations.

relationship: Sexual wrongdoing overtaken by its consequences
rationale: Sirach's adulterer is seized where he did not expect it; Proverbs describes lawless acts hunting a person and the cords of sins binding him, within its warning about another woman.
source_text: This man will receive retribution in the city’s squares and be seized where he did not suspect it.

target_units.text: Lawless acts hunt a man, and each is bound tight by the cords of his own sins.
He dies among the undisciplined; from the abundance of his own life he was cast out and perished through folly.

relationship: A wife joining another man during marriage
