rationale: Sirach condemns the wife leaving her husband and presenting another man's heir; Romans describes a woman belonging to another man while her husband lives as adulterous. The heir is Sirach's additional detail.
source_text: So also a woman who leaves her husband and presents an heir from another man.

target_units.text: For the married woman is bound by law to her living husband; but if the husband dies, she has been released from the law of the husband.

So then, while the husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she belongs to another man; but if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress when she belongs to another man.

relationship: Adultery as disobedience to God's law
rationale: Sirach explicitly names the woman's adultery as disobedience to the Most High's law; the native Exodus 20:13 gives the command against adultery.
source_text: For first she disobeyed the law of the Most High; second she wronged her husband; and third she committed adultery in sexual immorality and presented children from another man.

target_units.text: You shall not commit adultery.

relationship: Same-chapter elaboration of visitation upon offspring
rationale: The announcement of visitation upon the woman's children is followed by the image of children without a spreading root and branches without fruit. The later verse develops this stated consequence.
source_text: She will be brought before the assembly, and there will be a visitation upon her children.

target_units.text: Her children will not spread out into a root, and her branches will not bear fruit.

relationship: Unlawful offspring described by unstable roots and fruit
rationale: Sirach describes the children through roots that do not spread and fruitless branches; Wisdom likewise uses insecure roots and useless fruit for offspring from unlawful unions.
source_text: Her children will not spread out into a root, and her branches will not bear fruit.

target_units.text: But the prolific multitude of the ungodly will be of no use; from illegitimate shoots it will not send a root deep down, nor establish a secure foundation.
For even if it flourishes in branches for a time, standing insecurely, it will be shaken by wind and uprooted by the force of winds.
Unfulfilled branches will be broken off, and their fruit will be useless, unripe for eating, and fit for nothing.
For children born from unlawful unions are witnesses of wickedness against their parents at their examination.

relationship: Adultery's lasting reproach
rationale: Sirach predicts an unerased reproach and cursed memory for the adulterous woman; Proverbs describes the adulterer's dishonor and says his reproach will never be wiped away.
source_text: She will leave her memory as a curse, and her reproach will not be erased.

target_units.text: But the adulterer, through lack of sense, brings destruction upon his own life;
he bears pains and dishonors, and his reproach will never be wiped away.

relationship: The excellence of fearing God and the sweetness of His judgments
rationale: Sirach praises fear of the Lord and the sweetness of attending to His commandments; the psalm places enduring fear of the Lord beside judgments sweeter than honey and the reward of keeping them.
source_text: Those left behind will know that nothing is better than the fear of the Lord, and nothing sweeter than attending to the Lord’s commandments.

target_units.text: The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring for the age of the age; the Lord’s judgments are true, justified together,
desirable beyond gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and honeycomb.
For indeed, Thy servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great recompense.

relationship: Personified wisdom speaking publicly
rationale: Sirach introduces Wisdom praising herself among her people; Proverbs likewise presents Wisdom at public ways and gates, sending her voice to human beings.
source_text: Wisdom will praise her own soul and boast in the midst of her people.

target_units.text: For she is on the high summits, and stands between the paths.
For she sits beside the gates of rulers, and is praised at the entrances:
“You, O human beings, I summon, and I send forth my voice to the children of humankind.

relationship: Wisdom's public address
rationale: Wisdom opens her mouth before the Most High's assembly in Sirach; Proverbs presents her speaking at public gathering places to human beings. The audiences differ, but the speaking personification is shared.
source_text: She will open her mouth in the assembly of the Most High and boast before His host:

target_units.text: For she is on the high summits, and stands between the paths.
For she sits beside the gates of rulers, and is praised at the entrances:
“You, O human beings, I summon, and I send forth my voice to the children of humankind.

relationship: Wisdom coming forth from God
rationale: Sirach has Wisdom come from the Most High's mouth; Wisdom of Solomon calls her a breath of God's power and a pure outflow of His glory. Both portray her origin through an image of proceeding from God.
source_text: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High and covered the earth like mist.

target_units.text: For she is a breath of God’s power and a pure outflow of the Almighty’s glory; therefore nothing defiled enters into her.

relationship: The pillar of cloud
rationale: Wisdom locates her throne in a pillar of cloud; Exodus describes God's guidance of Israel in a pillar of cloud. The connection is the distinctive image of divine presence, without claiming that Exodus explicitly names Wisdom.
source_text: I dwelt in the heights, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud.

target_units.text: God led them by day in a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not cease before all the people.

relationship: Wisdom associated with the cosmic heights and depths
rationale: Sirach's Wisdom traverses heaven and the abyss; Proverbs describes her before the deeps and present with God as heaven and the world's springs are established.
source_text: Alone I encircled heaven’s circuit and walked in the depth of the abysses.

target_units.text: before making the earth and before making the deeps, before the springs of the waters came forth,
before the mountains were established, and before all hills He gives me birth.
The Lord made countries and uninhabited places, and the inhabited extremities of the world beneath heaven.
When He was preparing heaven, I was present with Him, and when He was marking out His own throne upon winds.
When He was making the clouds above strong, and when He was setting the springs of the world beneath heaven secure,
and was making the foundations of the earth strong,
I was beside Him, fitting things together; I was the one in whom He delighted. Day by day I rejoiced before Him at every time,

relationship: Wisdom's universal reach and rule
rationale: Sirach describes Wisdom's possession extending through sea, earth, and every people; Wisdom of Solomon says she reaches from end to end and governs all things well.
source_text: In the waves of the sea, in all the earth, and in every people and nation I gained possession.

target_units.text: She reaches mightily from end to end, and governs all things well.

relationship: Same-chapter search for a dwelling answered
rationale: Wisdom's search for rest and an inheritance in which to lodge receives the particular answer of the Creator settling her tent in Jacob and assigning her Israel as an inheritance.
source_text: Among all these I sought rest, and in whose inheritance I might lodge.

target_units.text: Then the Creator of all commanded me; my Creator settled my tent and said, ‘Dwell in Jacob, and receive your inheritance in Israel.’

relationship: Divine instruction entrusted particularly to Israel
rationale: Wisdom is commanded to dwell in Jacob and receive Israel as her inheritance; the psalm describes God's word and judgments being given to Jacob and Israel in a way not granted to every nation. Sirach 24:23 identifies the discourse with the law.
source_text: Then the Creator of all commanded me; my Creator settled my tent and said, ‘Dwell in Jacob, and receive your inheritance in Israel.’

target_units.text: He declares His word to Jacob, His ordinances and judgments to Israel.
He did not do so for any nation, and He did not disclose His judgments to them.

relationship: Wisdom created before the age
rationale: Both personifications speak of the Lord creating or founding Wisdom before the age. Proverbs expands this into a description of Wisdom before the earth, deeps, mountains, and hills.
source_text: Before the age, from the beginning, He created me, and for ever I will certainly not cease.

target_units.text: The Lord created me as the beginning of His ways, for His works.
Before the age He founded me, in the beginning,
before making the earth and before making the deeps, before the springs of the waters came forth,
before the mountains were established, and before all hills He gives me birth.

relationship: Zion as the chosen sacred dwelling
rationale: Wisdom's ministry in the holy tent and establishment in Zion correspond to the psalm's selection of Zion as the Lord's dwelling and its mention of His priests. The psalm speaks of the Lord's choice, not a separate statement by Wisdom.
source_text: I ministered before Him in the holy tent, and thus I was established in Zion.

target_units.text: For the Lord chose Zion; He selected her as His dwelling:
“This is My rest for age upon age; here I will dwell, for I selected her.
I will surely bless her game; I will satisfy her poor with loaves.
I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will surely exult.

relationship: The chosen place of dwelling in Zion
rationale: Wisdom describes being settled in the beloved city, Jerusalem; the psalm names Zion as the place the Lord selected for His dwelling and rest.
source_text: Likewise He settled me in the beloved city, and my authority was in Jerusalem.

target_units.text: For the Lord chose Zion; He selected her as His dwelling:
“This is My rest for age upon age; here I will dwell, for I selected her.

relationship: Jacob as the Lord's portion and inheritance
rationale: Sirach's description of the people as the Lord's portion and inheritance directly corresponds to Deuteronomy's naming of Jacob and Israel in those terms.
source_text: I took root in a glorified people, in the Lord’s portion, His inheritance.

target_units.text: And His people Jacob became the portion of the Lord; Israel, the measured lot of His inheritance.

relationship: Flourishing like a cedar of Lebanon
rationale: Wisdom's tall cedar of Lebanon image corresponds to the psalm's comparison of the righteous person's flourishing with a cedar in Lebanon.
source_text: I rose high like a cedar in Lebanon, like a cypress in the mountains of Hermon.

target_units.text: A righteous person will blossom like a palm tree; like the cedar in Lebanon he will multiply.

relationship: The flourishing olive-tree image
rationale: Sirach compares Wisdom to a stately olive among other trees; the psalmist compares himself to a fruitful olive in God's house. The shared image concerns flourishing, while the subjects and settings differ.
source_text: I rose high like a palm in En-gedi, like rose plants in Jericho, like a stately olive in the plain; I rose high like a plane tree.

target_units.text: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in God’s house; I hoped in God’s mercy for ever and for age upon age.

relationship: Fragrance using the sanctuary's incense ingredients
rationale: Sirach's description of Wisdom's scent names galbanum, onycha, stacte, and frankincense; Exodus lists these ingredients for holy incense placed before the testimonies in the tent.
source_text: Like cinnamon and aromatic aspalathus I gave a scent; like choice myrrh I spread fragrance, like galbanum, onycha, and stacte, and like a cloud of frankincense in a tent.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Moses, “Take to yourself spices: stacte, onycha, fragrant galbanum, and clear frankincense, in equal portions.
They shall make them into incense, a perfumer’s compound, blended, a pure and holy work.
Grind some of it fine and place it before the testimonies in the Tent of Testimony, where I will make Myself known to you. It shall be most holy to you.

relationship: Wisdom pictured as a tree
rationale: Wisdom's spreading terebinth branches form a tree image for her glory and grace; Proverbs likewise calls Wisdom a tree of life for those who hold her fast.
source_text: Like a terebinth I spread out my branches, and my branches were branches of glory and grace.

target_units.text: She is a tree of life to all who hold her fast, and secure for those who lean on her as on the Lord.

relationship: Vine blossom as an image of flourishing
rationale: Wisdom describes her gracious growth and blossoms through a vine; Hosea's restoration imagery similarly culminates in blossoming like a vine. Hosea applies the image to restored Israel rather than to personified Wisdom.
source_text: Like a vine I sprouted grace, and my blossoms were fruit of glory and wealth.

target_units.text: His branches will spread, and he will be like an olive tree laden with fruit; his fragrance will be like Lebanon.
They will return and settle beneath his shelter; they will live and be filled to intoxication with grain. His memorial will blossom like a vine, like Lebanon’s wine.

relationship: Wisdom inviting people to eat
rationale: Both personified Wisdom discourses invite hearers to come and receive nourishment: Sirach offers her produce, while Proverbs offers her bread and mixed wine and calls for leaving foolishness.
source_text: Come to me, you who desire me, and be filled from my produce.

target_units.text: “Whoever is foolish, let him turn aside to me!” And to those lacking understanding she said:
“Come, eat of my loaves, and drink wine that I mixed for you.
Leave foolishness, and you will live; seek understanding, so that you may live, and set insight right in knowledge.”

relationship: Instruction sweeter than honey
rationale: Wisdom calls her memory and inheritance sweeter than honey and honeycomb; the psalmist calls God's sayings sweeter than honey and honeycomb. Sirach's identification with the law in 24:23 makes the instructional connection explicit.
source_text: For my memory is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance than a honeycomb.

target_units.text: How sweet are Thy sayings to my throat, beyond honey and honeycomb to my mouth!

relationship: Contrasting hunger and thirst language
rationale: Sirach's Wisdom says those eating and drinking her will continue to hunger and thirst; Jesus, the bread of life, promises no hunger or thirst to those who come and believe. The paired images are close, while the stated outcomes contrast.
source_text: Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst.

target_units.text: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; the one who comes to Me will certainly never hunger, and the one who believes in Me will certainly never thirst.

relationship: Obedience, freedom from shame, and avoidance of sin
rationale: Wisdom promises that obedience avoids shame and working in her avoids sin; the psalm joins attention to God's commandments with freedom from shame and hiding His sayings in the heart to avoid sinning.
source_text: The one who obeys me will not be ashamed, and those who work in me will not sin.”

target_units.text: Then I will certainly not be ashamed when I look upon all Thy commandments.
I will give thanks unto Thee, Lord, with uprightness of heart, when I have learned Thy righteous judgments.
I will keep Thine ordinances; do not forsake me utterly.
Two: Beth. By what will the younger man set his way right? By keeping Thy words.
With my whole heart I sought Thee; do not thrust me away from Thy commandments.
In my heart I hid Thy sayings, so that I might not sin against Thee.

relationship: Direct correspondence in the law-as-inheritance wording
rationale: Sirach identifies the discourse with the law Moses commanded as an inheritance for Jacob's assemblies, closely reproducing the wording of Deuteronomy 33:4.
source_text: All these things are the book of the covenant of God Most High, the law which Moses commanded us as an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob,

target_units.text: the law which Moses commanded us, an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.

relationship: Eden's rivers in the picture of abundant wisdom
rationale: Sirach names the Pishon and Tigris in its flood image for wisdom; Genesis names both among the rivers flowing from Eden. The connection identifies the particular rivers, without making Genesis itself an allegory of wisdom.
source_text: which fills with wisdom like the Pishon, like the Tigris in the days of new crops,

target_units.text: And a river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides into four branches.
The name of the first is Pishon; it flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.
And the gold of that land is good; there also are the carbuncle and the green stone.
The name of the second river is Gihon; it flows around the whole land of Ethiopia.
The third river is the Tigris; it flows opposite Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

relationship: The Jordan at harvest as an abundance image
rationale: Sirach compares overflowing understanding to the Jordan in harvest days; Joshua explicitly describes the Jordan overflowing its bank during wheat harvest.
source_text: which fills with understanding like the Euphrates, like the Jordan in the days of harvest,

target_units.text: As the priests carrying the ark of the covenant entered the Jordan and the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord dipped into the edge of the Jordan’s water—the Jordan was overflowing its whole bank, as in the days of wheat harvest—

relationship: The named river Gihon
rationale: Sirach's comparison of instruction to the Gihon participates in the surrounding series of named rivers; Genesis identifies Gihon as one of Eden's rivers. The light and vintage comparisons remain Sirach's own imagery.
source_text: which makes instruction appear like light, like the Gihon in the days of vintage.

target_units.text: The name of the second river is Gihon; it flows around the whole land of Ethiopia.

relationship: Wisdom beyond complete human discovery
rationale: Sirach says neither the first nor the last traced Wisdom fully; Job describes wisdom as hidden from human beings while God knows its place.
source_text: The first did not come to know her fully, and likewise the last did not trace her out.

target_units.text: But where was wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding?
It has escaped every human and was hidden from the birds of heaven.
Destruction and Death said, ‘We have heard its renown.’
God established its way well, and He knows its place.

relationship: Same-chapter depths explaining Wisdom's untraceability
rationale: Wisdom's thought growing abundant from the sea and her counsel from a great abyss develop the preceding statement that neither first nor last has traced her fully. The connection concerns the explicitly stated limits of discovery.
source_text: For her thought grew abundant from the sea, and her counsel from a great abyss.

target_units.text: The first did not come to know her fully, and likewise the last did not trace her out.

relationship: Speech or teaching pictured as flowing water
rationale: Sirach's speaker compares himself to a river channel watering a garden; Proverbs compares a word in the heart to deep water and a springing river, a fountain of life.
source_text: I too came out like a channel from a river, like a watercourse into a garden.

target_units.text: A word in a man’s heart is deep water, and a river springs up, a fountain of life.

relationship: Same-chapter expansion of the teaching-water image
rationale: The channel and garden watercourse of the preceding verse grow into a river and sea as the speaker waters his garden. This is the deliberate expansion of the same water image.
source_text: I said, “I will water my garden and drench my garden bed.” Then behold, my channel became a river, and my river became a sea.

target_units.text: I too came out like a channel from a river, like a watercourse into a garden.

relationship: Instruction as illuminating light
rationale: Sirach promises to make instruction shine like dawn; Proverbs calls the law's commandment a lamp and light and joins it with correction and discipline.
source_text: I will again make instruction shine like the dawn and reveal these things far away.

target_units.text: because the commandment of law is a lamp and a light, and correction and discipline are life’s way,

relationship: Teaching preserved for future generations
rationale: Sirach's speaker promises to leave teaching for generations of ages; the psalm describes transmitting God's testimony and law so that children yet to be born will teach their own children.
source_text: I will again pour out teaching like prophecy and leave it for generations of ages.

target_units.text: it was not hidden from their children for another generation, as we announce the Lord’s praises, His mighty acts and the wonders He did.
And He raised a testimony in Jacob and set a law in Israel, whatever He commanded our fathers to make known to their sons,
so that another generation might know, sons who will be born; and they will rise and announce it to their sons,

relationship: Repeated declaration of labor for others
rationale: Both statements expressly say the speaker has labored not for himself alone but for others seeking wisdom or instruction.
source_text: See that I have labored not for myself alone, but for all who seek her.

target_units.text: Consider that I have labored not for myself alone, but for all who seek instruction.

relationship: The beauty of brothers dwelling in harmony
rationale: Sirach includes harmony among brothers among the relationships beautiful before God and people; the psalm praises brothers dwelling together as good and delightful.
source_text: In three things I was adorned and stood beautiful before the Lord and human beings: harmony among brothers, friendship among neighbors, and a wife and husband living agreeably with one another.

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. For David. Behold, what is good or what is delightful except for brothers to dwell together?

relationship: Learning in youth for wisdom in old age
rationale: The question about finding in old age what was not gathered in youth corresponds to the earlier instruction to choose discipline in youth and find wisdom until the hair is gray.
source_text: You have not gathered in youth; how could you find anything in your old age?

target_units.text: Child, choose instruction from your youth, and until your hair is gray you will find wisdom.

relationship: Wisdom and knowledge associated with long life
rationale: Sirach calls judgment and counsel fitting for gray-haired elders; Job associates wisdom with much time and knowledge with a long life.
source_text: How fitting is judgment for gray hair, and knowledge of counsel for elders!

target_units.text: In much time is wisdom, and in a long life knowledge.

relationship: Expectation of wisdom in age, with a qualification
rationale: Sirach calls wisdom fitting for the old and thought and counsel fitting for the honored; Elihu recounts expecting many years to bring wisdom, then qualifies this by denying that elders necessarily know judgment.
source_text: How fitting is wisdom for the old, and thought and counsel for the honored!

target_units.text: I said, ‘Time is what speaks, and in many years people know wisdom.’
But there is a spirit in mortals, and the Almighty’s breath is what teaches.
The long-lived are not wise, nor do elders know judgment.

relationship: Old age as a crown associated with reverence or righteousness
rationale: Sirach calls long experience the old person's crown and fear of the Lord his boast; Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in righteous ways.
source_text: Long experience is the crown of the old, and their boast is the fear of the Lord.

target_units.text: Old age is a crown of boasting, and it is found in ways of righteousness.

relationship: Rejoicing in one's children
rationale: Sirach includes a person rejoicing in children among the happy; Proverbs describes parental rejoicing over a wise son and urges the child to gladden father and mother. The enemy's fall is a separate clause.
source_text: Nine things I considered happy in my heart, and the tenth I will speak with my tongue: a person rejoicing in children, one who lives to see his enemies’ fall;

target_units.text: A righteous father brings up well, and his life rejoices over a wise son;
let father and mother rejoice over you, and let the one who bore you be glad.

relationship: The good wife and her husband's happiness
rationale: Sirach calls living with an understanding wife happy; chapter 26 similarly calls the good wife's husband happy and describes the gladness she brings. The target supports the marital clause.
source_text: happy is the one who lives with an understanding wife, who has not slipped with his tongue, and who has not served someone unworthy of him;

target_units.text: Happy is the husband of a good wife, and the number of his days is doubled.
A courageous wife gladdens her husband, and he will complete his years in peace.
A good wife is a good portion; she will be given among the portion of those who fear the Lord.

relationship: Happiness in finding understanding
rationale: Sirach calls the finder of prudence happy; Proverbs blesses the person who finds wisdom and sees good sense. This supports the first of the verse's two commendations.
source_text: happy is the one who has found prudence and the one who speaks into listening ears.

target_units.text: Blessed is the person who found wisdom, the mortal who saw good sense,

relationship: Fear of the Lord as wisdom's foundation
rationale: Sirach says that even a finder of wisdom is not above the person who fears the Lord; Proverbs makes fear of the Lord wisdom's beginning, connecting the two while giving fear a foundational role.
source_text: How great is the one who has found wisdom! Yet he is not above the one who fears the Lord.

target_units.text: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and the counsel of holy ones is understanding.

relationship: The preeminence of fearing the Lord
rationale: The statement that fear of the Lord surpasses everything corresponds to its earlier description as the crown of wisdom, making peace and healing flourish.
source_text: The fear of the Lord has surpassed everything; to whom will the one who holds it fast be compared?

target_units.text: The fear of the Lord is the crown of wisdom, making peace and the health of healing flourish.

relationship: Preference for harsh surroundings over a harmful marriage
rationale: Sirach prefers dwelling with a lion and dragon to an evil woman; Proverbs prefers desert dwelling to a battling, talkative, quick-tempered woman. Both express the comparison through an undesirable alternative dwelling.
source_text: I would choose to live with a lion and a dragon rather than live with an evil woman.

target_units.text: Better to dwell in a desert land than with a battling, talkative, and quick-tempered woman.

relationship: Same-chapter description of a husband's distress
rationale: The husband's involuntary bitter groaning among neighbors is further characterized in the chapter's description of an evil wife as a humbled heart, gloomy face, and wounded heart.
source_text: Her husband will recline among his neighbors and involuntarily groan bitterly.

target_units.text: An evil wife is a humbled heart, a gloomy face, and a wound of the heart; one who will not make her husband happy is slack hands and paralyzed knees.

relationship: A difficult marriage compared to adverse physical conditions
rationale: Sirach compares a talkative wife with a sandy ascent beneath an old person's feet; Proverbs compares an abusive wife with wintry drops driving a man from his house. The comparisons and descriptions of the wife differ.
source_text: A sandy ascent under an old person’s feet—so is a talkative wife to a quiet husband.

target_units.text: Drops drive a man from his house on a wintry day, and likewise an abusive wife from his own house.

relationship: Resisting desire aroused by beauty
rationale: Both warn against being overcome by desire for a woman's beauty. Proverbs adds being hunted by one's eyes and seized by her eyelids.
source_text: Do not fall for a woman’s beauty, and do not long for a woman.

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.

relationship: A harmful wife portrayed through bodily damage
rationale: Sirach describes an evil wife through a wounded heart, slack hands, and paralyzed knees; Proverbs likens a woman doing evil to a worm in wood destroying a man.
source_text: An evil wife is a humbled heart, a gloomy face, and a wound of the heart; one who will not make her husband happy is slack hands and paralyzed knees.

target_units.text: A courageous woman is a crown to her husband; but as a worm in wood, so a woman who does evil destroys a man.

relationship: An interpretation of sin and mortality in the Eden narrative
rationale: Sirach traces the beginning of sin and human death to the woman; God's sentence on Adam in Genesis connects his listening to his wife and eating with his eventual return to earth. Genesis also names Adam's own act of eating.
source_text: From a woman came the beginning of sin, and because of her we all die.

target_units.text: And to Adam He said: Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which alone I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your labours; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life.
Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and unto earth you shall return.

relationship: Contrast with the marital bond expressed as shared flesh
rationale: Sirach's instruction to cut the wife off from one's flesh reverses the unity expressed when Genesis calls the woman flesh of the man's flesh and the married pair one flesh. The target explains the marital image, not a rule endorsing Sirach's stated condition.
source_text: If she does not walk according to your direction, cut her off from your flesh.

target_units.text: And Adam said: This, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called Woman, for she was taken from her husband.
For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
